title: Hands-on: Three Operator Cases
points: Run one notebook to understand three operator studies.
180 minutes / three short exercises / no coding experience required
source_label: Setup: COLAB_GUIDE.md; Classroom_Labs.ipynb.
note: Open Classroom Labs before the workshop. Participants will run fresh numerical calculations and inspect clearly labeled archived model replies. Use the same notebook for all three cases. If devices are limited, work in pairs: one person runs the cells while the other checks the evidence. The deck uses the IEEE ComSoc theme. The classroom cycle is run, change, check and explain. This expanded edition includes a new L10B replay and a proposed control-room advisory pilot. The scheduled teaching time is 180 minutes; allow breaks outside that total. The presenter affiliations are supplied by the presenters. The new Stanford teaching bridge is an adaptation of general reliability ideas, not a claim that the lab implements those Stanford frameworks. Use the six-page Participant Lab Guide for the exact activity steps.

title: What would an operator ask an assistant to do?
points: Ask for a study: compare allowed options and show the checks needed for a decision.
The assistant returns a reviewable proposal linked to the input data and tool results.
note: Start with the operator’s job, not the model name. Read the illustrative request aloud. Ask participants to name the information they would need before making the study. This is a teaching design for an advisory assistant. The classroom notebook provides numerical counterparts for selected steps, not a live control-room connection.
caption: Illustrative study request and review path. The operator retains the decision.

title: What makes this an LLM agent?
points: A fixed script follows choices written in code. An LLM agent can choose a permitted next tool.
Both can branch and use the same solvers. We must test whether model choice adds value.
note: Use Anthropic’s attributed architectural distinction. A conventional program can contain feedback, branches, rules and sophisticated optimization. Those alone do not demonstrate an LLM agent. A generative model can also just write an explanation. In these records Llama makes bounded choices from an allowed list, receives tool evidence and may select another step. This is narrow agency, not unrestricted autonomy. The default class replays those choices.
caption: Same engineering tools, different source of the next-step choice. Both paths require checks.

title: Llama, Python and the operator have different jobs
points: Llama chooses and explains. Python calculates, checks limits and rejects failed proposals.
The operator reviews the evidence and decides whether another study or review is needed.
note: Llama is the language model, Ollama is the local service used to run it, and the application controls which tools can execute. Our recorded wrappers return schema-constrained JSON choices. They do not use Ollama’s native tool_calls protocol. Python validates and interprets the choice before calling numerical functions. Good JSON formatting does not make a claim physically correct. No classroom cell sends an equipment command.
caption: Roles in the recorded teaching workflow. The classroom route shows saved Llama choices.

title: An agent needs a goal, tools and a place to stop
points: Give the agent approved data, a small tool list and a saved record of what has been tried.
After each result, let it choose the next permitted step within explicit check and stop rules.
note: Walk around the loop once. State means the saved case record: input snapshot, selected candidate, tool outcomes and remaining study budget. A tool is an application function, such as running a power-flow check or solving a restoration problem. The engineering model, allowed actions, limits and stop conditions belong to the application. A model can request REVIEW when the permitted route cannot resolve a problem. In the original P3 record only two candidate checks are allowed.
caption: Teaching model of a bounded agent. Each result updates the case record before the next choice.

title: Break one big request into small jobs
points: Ask for one clear result at each step. Save it so the next step can use it.
In our lab, Python calculates and checks. L10B shows how Llama selected a next step.
note: Stanford connection: Lam’s CS224V introduction, pp.19–20, uses WikiChat to illustrate splitting a response into retrieval, claim checking and writing. Our diagram is an original power-system teaching adaptation. Follow the voltage path: read the current allowance, choose a permitted candidate, calculate its result, check limits and explain the outcome. This is an analogy across domains, not evidence that WikiChat is a power-system controller. Ask pairs to name which step would detect a current violation.
caption: Original teaching adaptation of the task-decomposition idea. The notebook does not run WikiChat.
source_label: Monica Lam, CS224V Lecture 1, pp.19–20; Semnani et al., WikiChat (2023).

title: Find the rule, then test the result
points: A document can tell us the limit. A numerical tool tells us how the proposal compares with it.
Keep the source, the measured or calculated value, and the remaining checks together.
note: Stanford connection: the lecture’s WikiChat discussion, pp.17–25, separates finding material from checking factual claims. Apply the habit to a grid study: retrieving a current limit is different from calculating current for a candidate. The displayed 99.604410% value belongs to the separate archived P3 OpenDSS replay, not to the learner’s fresh L2 result. This example supports only that current check under its recorded model. A sentence, retrieved document or citation does not establish full-network feasibility.
caption: Teaching analogy. The number shown comes from the recorded P3 replay, which is separate from L2.
source_label: Monica Lam, CS224V Lecture 1, pp.17–25; recorded P3 current check.

title: Tell the agent what is allowed
points: Write down the goal, required inputs, permitted tools and stop rules before the study.
If something required is missing, report what is missing and keep the proposal on HOLD.
note: Stanford connection: Lam p.40 and the published Genie Worksheets paper emphasize developer-defined workflows and knowledge sources. The published framework uses an algorithmic runtime to enforce a supplied policy, with LLMs used for language understanding and response generation. Our lab uses custom Python functions, not Genie Worksheets. The application analogy is to specify the task and prevent a language reply from silently changing its limits or filling missing required inputs. A passed calculation does not prove that the task description was correct.
caption: Original teaching analogy to Genie Worksheets. This lab uses Python and does not implement Genie.
source_label: Monica Lam, CS224V Lecture 1, p.40; Joshi et al., Genie Worksheets (ACL 2025).

title: A useful explanation makes a claim we can check
points: Read the returned reason. Identify its evidence and the tool result that could support it.
A clear explanation can still be wrong. Keep the numerical check and the original reply.
note: We show only the public reasons returned in the recorded JSON. We do not expose or infer private internal reasoning. Ask whether the statement matches the input, respects the allowed choices and survives the numerical check. Later the restoration reply says it sorted costs correctly while returning the wrong order. That specific error is an opportunity to inspect the application’s guard.
caption: Check the explanation against the recorded facts and tool output.

title: Six terms we will use in the notebook
points: Each term describes one job. The language model chooses among tools that do these jobs.
A passing result applies only to the inputs, limits and parts of the network that were checked.
note: MPC plans controls using a forecast. SAC supplies a proposal from a previously trained controller. MILP chooses whole loads while respecting the stated constraints. WLS finds the state that best fits the weighted readings. Evidence binding checks that inputs and command still match a stored result. Model scope means which network parts and physical effects were included. Also define p.u. as a value divided by its stated base: 1.0 p.u. is that base value. A thermal limit here is a current or flow limit. The objective or cost is the numerical score to optimize after required checks pass.
caption: Plain-language meanings. The detailed equations stay in the notebooks and source guide.

title: Know what is running and what is being replayed
points: Green: run a numerical calculation now. Amber: read an actual saved Llama reply in L10B.
Blue: discuss a proposed advisory pilot for a control room after the hands-on work.
note: Point to these evidence modes throughout the session. Default classroom cells calculate fresh results without a live language-model call. L10B displays verified historical Llama choices, original reasons and associated recorded results. Changing your L2 or L6 input does not change those old replies. The final control-room diagrams are a proposed teaching design, not evidence of a deployed utility platform. No new equipment operation occurs in any of these modes.
caption: Three explicitly labeled teaching modes used throughout this workshop.

title: Colab is a workbook with a computer attached
points: The notebook holds instructions, code and outputs. A temporary computer runs the code.
Save your notebook copy. After a runtime reset, rerun setup and the earlier cells.
note: Explain the picture before using any interface terms. An .ipynb file is the workbook. The runtime is a temporary computer supplied by Colab. Variables and files in its temporary storage are separate from the notebook file. Saving a copy in Drive or downloading the notebook keeps its text, code and saved outputs; it does not keep the whole temporary computer. There is no need to mount the user’s Drive for this lab. The setup cell retrieves the required source and records. We use a CPU runtime and no live language-model service.
caption: Notebook file and temporary runtime are different. Google Colab FAQ; original illustration.
source_label: Google Colab FAQ: notebook storage, execution state and temporary virtual machines.

title: Run L1: does the evidence still match?

note: Evidence binding means matching a checked record to the exact inputs, proposed command and returned result, using content hashes. A matching hash also does not authenticate a sensor.

title: Voltage: open L2
points: MPC makes a forecast-based plan. SAC is a saved learned controller.
Check limits first. Then compare penalty score J; smaller is preferred after the checks pass.
source_label: Classroom_Labs.ipynb, L2; cell classroom-007; src/continuous_control.py.
note: The feeder is a synthetic SMART-DS Greensboro-area example, not a measured utility circuit. The command sets active- and reactive-power participation for an inverter fleet. MPC, model predictive control, uses a system model and a short forecast to calculate a plan under limits; here the proposed command is the first step of that plan. SAC, Soft Actor–Critic, is a saved controller learned from rewards. It produces a proposal from old weights without training again. The default calculation covers medium-voltage (MV) phases and MV line currents, with simplified low-voltage (LV) aggregation. Feasible means the proposal passes the limits represented by that model. Compare the penalty score J only after checking those limits; smaller J is preferred for this stated objective. Run L0 and L1 first.
caption: Synthetic SMART-DS teaching feeder; not an operating utility circuit.

title: Control settings and limits
points: a sets active-power participation; b sets reactive-power participation.
Check the inverter limits, modeled voltages and allowed line current.
source_label: Classroom_Labs.ipynb, L2; cell classroom-007; src/continuous_control.py.
note: Active power delivers net energy; reactive power supports the AC voltage and current balance. The command uses P_i = a S_i and Q_i = b S_i. Its bounds are 0 <= a <= 1, |b| <= 0.44 and a^2 + b^2 <= 1. Modeled voltages must be between 0.95 and 1.05 per unit (p.u.), where values are divided by a stated base. RATING_FRACTION=0.80 sets allowed current to 80% of the nominal rating. The displayed current percentage uses this reduced allowance as its denominator. Passing the inverter bounds alone does not show that network limits pass.
caption: Active and reactive settings share the inverter’s power limit.

title: Run L2 with the default inputs
points: Run all of L2 to calculate the MPC plan and check the saved SAC controller’s proposal.
Read feasible, current_step_J and max_allowed_current_pct.
source_label: Classroom_Labs.ipynb, L2; cell classroom-007; src/continuous_control.py.
note: Start with LOAD_SCALE=1.0 and RATING_FRACTION=0.80. The saved SAC actor produces a new proposal by inference; it is not trained in this cell. Both proposals pass the default classroom checks. MPC has the lower current-step J for this case and objective. This single result does not establish a universal control advantage. The output field feasible reports whether the modeled limits pass; current_step_J is this step’s penalty score, and max_allowed_current_pct is maximum current as a percentage of the reduced allowance.

title: Read the voltage and current plots
points: Left: compare the sorted modeled voltages with the allowed band.
Right: compare line current with the 100% allowed-current limit.
source_label: Classroom_Labs.ipynb, L2; cell classroom-007; src/continuous_control.py.
note: The left panel sorts each voltage curve separately. The same horizontal position means the same rank, not necessarily the same physical bus. The right panel reports current relative to the reduced allowance. Use the output table for exact extrema and feasibility; do not decide acceptance from a plot alone.
caption: Reference L2 plots; rerun L2 to calculate plots for your inputs.

title: Check limits before comparing scores
points: Default MPC passes: current use 73.62%, penalty score J about 0.03110.
Default saved SAC passes: current use 51.68%, J about 0.43643.
source_label: Classroom_Labs.ipynb, L2; cell classroom-007; src/continuous_control.py.
note: In the reference execution, MPC returns a=0.960307 and b=-0.111114, with Vmin=1.023874 and Vmax=1.038709 p.u. SAC returns a=0.340066 and b=0.014024, with Vmin=1.013243 and Vmax=1.030000 p.u. Values may vary slightly with the solver or dependency version. Lower current use need not mean lower J, because the objective also includes service and control terms. Check feasibility before comparing J. Both voltage extrema are within the stated 0.95–1.05 p.u. band for this represented MV model.
caption: Reference L2 output with LOAD_SCALE=1.0 and RATING_FRACTION=0.80.

title: Exercise 1: tighten the current allowance
points: In L2, change only RATING_FRACTION from 0.80 to 0.75. Predict, then rerun.
For each method, report feasible, allowed-current use and current_step_J.
Does a PASS cover the full medium- and low-voltage network? Explain.
source_label: Classroom_Labs.ipynb, L2; cell classroom-007; src/continuous_control.py.
note: Allow one minute to predict, two minutes to edit and run, and one minute to report. Keep LOAD_SCALE=1.0. Reference allowed-current use is 78.527895% for MPC and 54.854158% for SAC; both remain feasible. Do not ask learners to find a rejection that this edit does not produce. The default model still covers MV only.

title: Debrief: both proposals still pass
points: At 0.75, both pass: MPC uses about 78.53% of the allowance; SAC uses about 54.85%.
The tighter allowance raises current use as a percentage, but does not cause failure here.
source_label: Classroom_Labs.ipynb, L2; cell classroom-007; src/continuous_control.py.
note: An incorrect prediction is useful evidence, not a failed exercise. Compare the hypothesis with the actual output. Both candidates retain enough headroom in this case. An optimizer may change its command when a constraint changes, so a simple fixed-ratio argument does not apply to every scenario. The model scope has not expanded.

title: Change one number and explain the difference
points: A smaller current allowance makes the same current a larger percentage of that allowance.
Record the new percentage and check whether it still stays below 100%.
note: Use this visual immediately after the first exercise debrief. It shows the measured reference MPC outputs, rounded to two decimal places, for RATING_FRACTION 0.80 and 0.75. The SAC result is also computed in the notebook but is not drawn here. Both proposals pass this particular tighter test. The result is not a general guarantee for other loads or limits. Ask pairs to explain the denominator in the percentage. Restore the default before moving to L3’s independent archived case.
caption: Reference L2 exercise: MPC uses 73.62% of the default allowance and 78.53% after the change.
source_label: Classroom Labs L2, cell classroom-007; verified default and exercise outputs.

title: Restoration: open L6
points: Use the six-node teaching graph. Keep the faulted branch unavailable.
Compare total restored load with restored critical load.
source_label: Classroom_Labs.ipynb, L6; cell classroom-018; src/standard_formulations.py.
note: This six-node graph is separate from the voltage feeder. It represents active-power transport, not AC power flow or a time-ordered field switching procedure. Loads are picked up as whole blocks. A tie is an alternative connection that can supply load; CAPACITIES_KW sets its transfer limit in kilowatts.
caption: Six-node active-power teaching graph with whole-load pickup and one unavailable branch.

title: Choose the service goal before the plan
points: The priority goal gives more weight to two critical loads.
The comparison goal serves the most total kW, using the same network and pickup rules.
source_label: Classroom_Labs.ipynb, L6; cell classroom-018; src/standard_formulations.py.
note: Critical demand totals 90 kW: 60 kW at node 2 and 30 kW at node 5. The objective is the service goal encoded as a score. The priority score gives more weight to these critical loads, while the comparison score maximizes total kW. The difference in selected service comes from that goal. Both numerical methods use the same graph, capacities and whole-load pickup rules. Neither needs a language model to solve this declared problem.
caption: Different service goals can select different loads on the same network.

title: Run L6: change the tie capacity
points: Run all of L6. MILP chooses whole loads; an exhaustive search checks its priority score.
Read served_kw, critical_kw and MILP_matches_exhaustive_check.
source_label: Classroom_Labs.ipynb, L6; cell classroom-018; src/standard_formulations.py.
note: MILP means mixed-integer linear programming. Here it is a whole-load chooser: on/off choices decide which load blocks are served, while linear constraints enforce the stated network rules. Start with tie capacities of 40, 60, 80, 100 and 120 kW. The solver enforces active-power balance, capacity limits, connection to a source, no loops in the energized graph, and exclusion of the faulted branch. points: An approved interface supplies read-only data and study tools. Log every request and result.
Keep equipment commands in the utility’s separate authorized operating process.
note: Proposed advisory pilot. Walk through the lanes: operator, assistant, application-controlled tool gateway and engineering tools. Llama requests one permitted function; the application checks the request and executes the tool. A snapshot identifier binds the result to the input. The workshop Python functions are teaching counterparts, not SCADA adapters. NIST OT guidance supports controlled information flows, least privilege and logging. The exact pilot architecture is our teaching recommendation, not a NIST-certified design.
caption: Proposed advisory pilot — teaching design. Classroom functions are not live control-room interfaces.
source_label: Teaching proposal informed by NIST OT guidance and the cited notebook checks.

title: Check three things before returning a proposal
points: Check that the inputs match, the required limits pass and the required network parts were modeled.
Example: an MV-only PASS stays on HOLD when the request requires the full MV/LV network.
note: Proposed advisory pilot. Current data and a matching evidence packet are the first gate. The second gate checks stated engineering limits with approved tools. The third asks whether the calculations cover the request, including excluded low-voltage parts or required protection and dynamic studies. This is not a universal complete security checklist. It illustrates why L12 can produce a passing local calculation and still HOLD a broader request. Make missing evidence visible instead of allowing fluent text to fill the gap.
caption: Proposed advisory pilot — teaching design. A PASS is limited to its tested model and inputs.
source_label: Teaching proposal informed by NIST OT guidance and the cited notebook checks.

title: Give the operator a short evidence packet
points: Show the input snapshot, selected option, worst margins, rejected trials and missing checks.
The reviewer can ask for another study, reject the proposal or accept it for the next review step.
note: Proposed advisory pilot. Use three review questions: Does this match the current equipment, inputs and model? Did the required checks pass, with missing checks clear? What exactly am I approving, who owns the next step, and where is the record? Record the reviewer, reason, case snapshot and tool versions. Accepting a study result does not itself issue an equipment command. Authorized operating procedures and roles determine any later physical action. L12 practices only a simulated ID-bound readback.
caption: Proposed advisory pilot — teaching design. Review of a study is distinct from operating equipment.
source_label: Teaching proposal informed by NIST OT guidance and the cited notebook checks.

title: Adopt it in stages and measure the benefit
points: Begin with past cases, then read-only shadow work, then a limited pilot with named reviewers.
Compare against the same tools in a fixed script: correct studies, missed checks, time and rework.
note: Proposed advisory pilot. Historical replay lets engineers define expected outcomes and failure cases. Shadow use compares recommendations alongside the existing process without relying on them for equipment control. A limited pilot needs a named owner, training, an agreed scope and a way to stop use. Measure end-to-end elapsed time including review, correct completed studies, missed or stale inputs, overlooked limits and reviewer changes. Compare the same engineering tools with and without Llama. Our paired records show identical final numerical results, so there is no basis yet to promise higher accuracy, less operator workload or faster decisions. NIST AI RMF supports human roles, evaluation under realistic conditions and deactivation; these particular pilot metrics are our recommendation.
caption: Proposed advisory pilot — teaching design. Benefits must be measured against an appropriate baseline.
source_label: Teaching proposal informed by NIST OT guidance and the cited notebook checks.
